strengths: Addresses the useful and underexplored problem of text-to-video generation with an alpha channel, including difficult semi-transparent effects, fine boundaries, and temporally varying transparency.

The proposed system is technically coherent: a causal feature-merging module places RGB and alpha information in a shared latent space, alpha-aware rendering losses train the VAE, and parameter-efficient adaptation reuses a strong pretrained video model.

The qualitative examples are diverse and often visibly sharper and more detailed than the displayed TransPixeler outputs. The reported 4-step generation and 128-second runtime for 81 frames also suggest meaningful practical potential.

The manuscript is generally clear, describes the principal architecture and objectives, acknowledges characteristic failure cases, and provides useful implementation details such as resolution, ranks, iterations, and batch sizes.
weaknesses: The central superiority claims are not supported by quantitative evaluation or a user study. There are no measurements of alpha reconstruction, temporal consistency, prompt alignment, perceptual quality, or motion quality, and no uncertainty or multi-seed analysis. Static frame strips are especially insufficient for judging video motion and temporal alpha stability.

The comparison is not adequately controlled. Wan-Alpha frequently receives substantially more detailed prompts and additional style, shot, and transparency instructions, while TransPixeler receives short English prompts; Wan-Alpha is evaluated with Chinese prompts and a different base model. Output length, resolution, frame rate, sampling configuration, and acceleration also differ, so neither quality nor the claimed approximately 15x speedup is an apples-to-apples comparison.

There are no ablations isolating the proposed contributions: feature merging, causal modules, soft versus hard rendering losses, Sobel/perceptual losses, DoRA versus LoRA, data curation, and LightX2V four-step inference. Consequently, it is unclear whether gains arise from the method, the stronger Wan backbone, prompt engineering, curated examples, or external acceleration.

The VAE itself receives no reconstruction evaluation or comparison with LayerDiffuse/AlphaVAE-style alternatives. The feature merger is trained without a KL constraint, but the compatibility and distribution of its latents are not analyzed. Alpha masks are rarely shown directly, making semi-transparency and boundary correctness difficult to verify.

Evaluation breadth is narrow: only one competing method is tested despite several relevant transparent-video methods discussed in the related work, and the qualitative samples may be selectively chosen. Failure frequency and performance across transparent-object categories are not reported.

Reproducibility is incomplete. Optimizer settings, learning rates, loss weights or normalization, DoRA/LoRA insertion locations, hardware, inference scheduler, seeds, and precise speed protocol are absent. The text-to-video set contains only 437 curated samples, including unspecified Internet data, but sample provenance, licensing, splits, and release details are unclear; the manuscript's model website link is also blank.

The claim of no extra inference cost is overstated: although adapter weights can be merged, producing RGB and alpha requires duplicated decoder execution. Overall, the application and qualitative results are promising, but the missing controlled evaluation is a consequential scientific weakness that currently outweighs the contribution.

strengths: The paper addresses a useful and relatively underexplored problem: efficient text-to-video generation with a jointly produced alpha channel, including semi-transparent effects and fine boundaries.

The proposed system is practically simple: it adapts a strong pretrained Wan model through a shared RGBA latent representation, decoder LoRAs, and a diffusion-transformer DoRA instead of duplicating the main generation backbone.

The displayed examples are qualitatively promising and cover people, animals, hair, glass, glow, smoke, and other effects. Several examples appear visibly sharper and more detailed than the shown TransPixeler outputs.

The manuscript describes the main architecture, rendering losses, data sources, and basic training configuration clearly, and it acknowledges failure cases involving alpha-mask holes and unintended foreground debris.
weaknesses: The central superiority claims are not supported by quantitative evaluation. There are no alpha reconstruction or compositing metrics, temporal-consistency measures, text-alignment or video-quality metrics, benchmark aggregates, or human preference studies. Claims about visual quality, motion realism, alpha accuracy, and state-of-the-art performance therefore rest entirely on selected frame sequences.

The comparison protocol is materially unfair and insufficiently specified. Wan-Alpha frequently receives much richer prompts than TransPixeler—for example, added appearance, framing, and style descriptions—while the baselines receive short prompts. The paper also does not report prompt count, random seeds, samples generated per prompt, selection policy, or baseline inference settings. Selected frames cannot establish motion consistency or exclude cherry-picking.

The text-to-video model is trained on only 437 curated samples, yet no held-out evaluation split, training-data overlap analysis, or nearest-neighbor/memorization study is provided. Given this extremely small dataset and the semantic similarity between some training and showcased categories, generalization beyond the curated examples is not demonstrated.

No ablation study isolates the contributions of the feature-merging block, causal modules, hard/soft rendering objectives, edge and perceptual losses, DoRA instead of LoRA, data filtering, or four-step acceleration. The VAE itself is not compared quantitatively with LayerDiffuse or AlphaVAE. Consequently, the proposed design choices and their claimed benefits cannot be attributed reliably.

The efficiency evidence is not reproducible or apples-to-apples. The claimed 15× speedup compares videos with different frame counts, resolutions, frame rates, architectures, and apparently sampling configurations; the device is not identified. Moreover, claiming no extra computational cost is misleading because inference explicitly duplicates the VAE decoder to produce RGB and alpha outputs, even if adapter weights can be merged.

Reproducibility is inadequate: optimizer and learning-rate settings, Wan model variant, adapter target layers, feature-merge depth, attention configuration, sampling details, prompt-extension procedure, baseline settings, hardware, and dataset filtering rules are omitted. Additional Internet data are unspecified, including provenance and licensing, and the stated model website is blank in the submitted manuscript.

Methodological originality is limited. Much of the pipeline combines established components—LayerDiffuse-style latent transparency, a pretrained Wan backbone, LoRA/DoRA adaptation, rectified flow, and LightX2V acceleration. The feature-merging VAE adaptation may be useful, but without ablations or reconstruction results its technical contribution is not established strongly enough to offset the evaluation deficiencies.

Overall, the work has practical promise and visually encouraging examples, but the absence of controlled, aggregate evidence is consequential rather than a presentation-level issue. The manuscript does not currently substantiate its principal quality, generalization, and efficiency claims to the standard required for acceptance.

strengths: The paper addresses a practically important and comparatively underexplored problem: efficient text-to-video generation with a jointly generated alpha channel. The demonstrated applications to compositing, effects, hair, glass, glow, and semi-transparent materials are relevant to computer-vision and content-creation workflows.

The central design is pragmatic and potentially useful: alpha information is merged into the pretrained Wan-VAE latent space, while decoder LoRAs and a diffusion-transformer DoRA adapt a strong RGB video model without duplicating the diffusion backbone. This should make the method easier to deploy than architectures requiring a second backbone.

The VAE objective thoughtfully combines direct alpha reconstruction with soft- and hard-rendered RGB supervision, perceptual loss, and edge loss. Random background colors are a sensible way to discourage conflating transparency with a particular RGB background.

The qualitative results are strong. Across the displayed examples, Wan-Alpha generally produces sharper, more detailed subjects than TransPixeler, including convincing fine structures and challenging transparent or emissive content. The sequences also suggest useful temporal motion rather than merely static-image animation.

The system offers an attractive practical operating point: 480x832 output, 81 frames, and four-step generation without classifier-free guidance. The reported 128-second runtime is substantially below the reported TransPixeler runtime on the same device.

The manuscript is organized clearly, provides understandable architecture diagrams, states key adapter ranks and training iteration counts, and candidly illustrates failure modes involving alpha-mask holes and unwanted debris.
weaknesses: The experimental evidence is almost entirely qualitative. There are no quantitative measures of alpha accuracy, temporal consistency, text alignment, perceptual quality, motion quality, or human preference, and no uncertainty or sample count is reported. Consequently, the broad claim of superior visual quality, motion realism, and transparency rendering is not established beyond a small set of selected examples.

The baseline comparison is not controlled. Wan-Alpha receives substantially expanded prompts containing shot, style, appearance, and motion details, whereas TransPixeler is often given only a short phrase; Wan-Alpha is also prompted in Chinese while the baselines use English. These differences can materially affect quality and semantic fidelity, so the figures do not isolate the contribution of the method.

No ablation studies evaluate the feature-merging block, causal modules, random hard rendering, soft versus hard rendering losses, perceptual and edge losses, DoRA versus LoRA, data filtering, or four-step acceleration. This makes it difficult to determine which proposed components are necessary or whether simpler alternatives would perform similarly.

The efficiency claim is insufficiently substantiated. The paper omits the GPU model, precision, memory use, software settings, sampling-step count for TransPixeler, and repeated timing protocol. The compared outputs also differ in resolution, frame count, and frame rate. Moreover, generating RGB and alpha with two decoder copies is not literally free; merging adapters removes adapter overhead but does not remove the second decoding pass.

Reproducibility is limited. Important details such as optimizer, learning rate and schedule, loss weights, feature-merge depth and attention configuration, preprocessing, LightX2V settings, prompt-extension procedure, compute budget, and random-seed/evaluation protocol are absent.

The data description is not sufficiently auditable. The diffusion model uses only 437 selected samples, including 116 unspecified Internet videos, while the stated 77,237 VAE training videos appear partly derived from static images and temporal-window augmentation. The manuscript does not report unique-source counts, licensing, deduplication, train/test overlap checks, or a held-out prompt suite.

The technical novelty is moderate: much of the system combines established ingredients—LayerDiffuse-style latent transparency, a pretrained Wan backbone, LoRA/DoRA, standard reconstruction/perceptual/edge losses, and an existing four-step acceleration framework. The feature-merging VAE adaptation is useful, but its advantage over prior RGBA VAE designs is not quantitatively demonstrated.

There are smaller clarity issues, including the unsupported assertion that causal 3D convolution is computationally cheaper than conventional 3D convolution, ambiguity about applying VGG perceptual loss to alpha videos, and a missing model/project URL. These are presentation or documentation refinements rather than the main decision-driving concerns.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and relatively underexplored problem: direct generation of RGBA videos, including semi-transparent phenomena that ordinary foreground segmentation or post-hoc matting cannot represent well.

The proposed adaptation is practically attractive. It retains the pretrained Wan2.1-14B DiT architecture, confines additional modeling largely to the VAE adapters, DoRA parameters, and noise initialization, and reports substantially faster inference than TransPixeler.

Using both a transparency-aware latent objective and a spatially varying noise mean is an interesting formulation. The Gaussian ellipse interface also offers intuitive control over approximate foreground position and scale.

The manuscript is generally clear and visually polished. It provides comparisons with four prior-system configurations, a generation-plus-matting baseline, reconstruction ablations, and qualitative control examples.

The reported results are promising: the method leads all compared systems in the listed VBench/VLM metrics and receives substantially better average user-study ranks for transparency and overall quality.
weaknesses: There is a material inconsistency in the rectified-flow formulation. Equation (2) correctly defines the velocity for Z_t=t epsilon+(1-t)Z as epsilon-Z, whereas Equation (13) defines the modified target as Z_t-epsilon=(1-t)(Z-epsilon), which reverses and time-scales that velocity. If Equation (13) reflects the implementation, the stated sampling/training derivation is incorrect; if it is a typo, the algorithm is still not reproducible as written.

The central bidirectional loss is insufficiently justified. Multiplying a nonnegative squared error by -1 in transparent regions makes that component unbounded below and explicitly rewards arbitrarily poor predictions by the frozen DiT. The paper provides neither a stabilizing bound nor loss weights, gradient treatment, or an analysis showing that this objective specifically separates alpha information rather than exploiting the frozen model.

Evidence for the main transparency claim is weak. Transparency correctness is assessed only through an underspecified ranking study: the manuscript omits the number and expertise of raters, number and selection of prompts/videos, randomization, agreement, uncertainty, and significance. No objective alpha-quality or compositing-based metric is reported.

The overall evaluation protocol is substantially underspecified. The test prompt count and provenance, number of random seeds, VLM prompt/rubric, GPT-4o version, and confidence intervals are absent. The considerably different backbone capacities and inference settings of the systems are also not controlled, so improvements cannot be cleanly attributed to the proposed distribution-learning components rather than Wan2.1-14B and the acceleration pipeline.

The ablations do not adequately support the generation claims. Table 3 measures VAE reconstruction, not generated-video quality or latent disentanglement; the mean sampler and full TABD contribution are evaluated only through a few static examples. There are no quantitative generation ablations, distribution analyses, or comparisons with simpler unsigned/margin-based alternatives.

Reproducibility is limited by missing thresholds defining opaque, semi-transparent, and transparent regions; loss coefficients; optimizer and learning-rate schedules; ellipse edge cases; preprocessing details; and evaluation splits. The generation dataset contains only 429 curated samples, including unspecified Internet data, but the paper does not establish a disjoint test set or rule out source overlap. Promised supplementary material, model, and dataset access are not available in the submitted manuscript.

Static figures look favorable, but they cannot substantiate claims about motion, temporal stability, or flicker, and several qualitative conclusions rely on isolated examples. Taken together with the mathematical ambiguity and incomplete evaluation, these issues outweigh the paper's useful idea in its current form.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and relatively underexplored problem: directly generating temporally coherent RGB-A video, including semi-transparent phenomena such as glass, smoke, lighting, and hair.

The proposed system is practically attractive. It adapts a strong pretrained video model without expanding the DiT backbone, supports spatial control through an inference-time mask, and is reported to generate 81 frames in 128 seconds—substantially faster than TransPixeler.

The alpha-aware VAE, rendering-based reconstruction objectives, and shifted-noise conditioning form a reasonably coherent pipeline. Comparisons include several RGB-A generators, a generation-plus-matting alternative, component ablations, and both text-to-video and image-to-video demonstrations.

The reported results consistently favor the proposed model, including text alignment, aesthetics, temporal metrics, and user preferences. The qualitative examples also suggest better foreground structure and alpha boundaries than several baselines.
weaknesses: The rectified-flow formulation contains a consequential technical inconsistency. Given Z_t=t·epsilon+(1-t)·Z, the target velocity should be epsilon-Z, as correctly stated in Eq. (2). Equation (13), however, defines the modified velocity as Z_t-epsilon=(1-t)(Z-epsilon), which has the wrong sign and an unintended time-dependent scale. The paper does not clarify whether this is merely a notation error or the objective actually used in the reported experiments.

The central bidirectional loss is insufficiently justified and potentially unstable. Equation (3) multiplies squared error by -1 in non-opaque regions, so minimizing it explicitly maximizes an unbounded prediction error with respect to the trainable VAE. No weighting, normalization, stability mechanism, or optimization analysis is given. Moreover, the claimed equivalence between prediction error and latent likelihood is asserted rather than derived.

The evidence does not isolate or validate the main distribution-shifting claim. Table 3 reports only reconstruction metrics, which do not establish improved RGB/alpha separability, likelihood behavior, or downstream generation quality. The generation ablation is a single qualitative example, with no quantitative ablation of TABD, the mean sampler, mean-shift training versus inference-only masking, or preservation of the base model's RGB capability.

The evaluation protocol is too underspecified to support the broad superiority claims. The manuscript omits the number and source of test prompts, sampling procedure, random seeds, number and expertise of user-study participants, repetitions, agreement, confidence intervals, and significance testing. Transparency—the principal contribution—is evaluated only through an undocumented ranking study, while the automatic metrics are computed after compositing onto white and therefore cannot directly measure alpha correctness.

Baseline comparability is unclear. The methods use different base generators, model scales, resolutions, frame counts, and likely training data; the paper does not control for these factors or report matched compute and parameter counts. Consequently, improvements in RGB-oriented metrics may substantially reflect the strong Wan2.1-14B backbone rather than the proposed RGB-A mechanisms.

Reproducibility is weak. Important details are deferred to unavailable supplementary material, including optimizer settings, learning rates, loss weights, threshold definitions for opaque/semi-transparent/transparent regions, prompt sets, evaluation code, and user-study design. The generation dataset has only 429 selected samples, including 85 Internet videos whose provenance and licensing are unspecified. The ellipse construction is also undefined for empty or singleton foreground masks.

There are smaller clarity problems, including inconsistent claims about whether the Gaussian mean is shifted in transparent regions even though G is fitted to pixels with alpha greater than 0.5, overloaded use of the symbol mu, and several claims of causality that exceed the presented ablations. These are secondary to the technical and evidential concerns above.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and underexplored problem—temporally consistent RGB-A video generation—with clear value for compositing, filmmaking, games, and UI content creation.

The proposed adaptation is practically attractive: it retains the pretrained Wan2.1-T2V-14B backbone, keeps the latent dimensionality unchanged, and adds relatively lightweight VAE LoRA/merging components, DiT DoRA, and shifted-noise sampling.

The combination of rendering-aware VAE training, transparency-aware latent learning, and spatial control through a Gaussian ellipse mask is technically interesting and more comprehensive than simply attaching an image-based RGB-A VAE to a video model.

The reported results are promising. The method leads all evaluated baselines in Table 1, including text alignment (4.00), aesthetic quality (0.649), motion smoothness (0.9949), and temporal-flickering score (0.9941). The qualitative examples also show convincing fine boundaries and semi-transparent effects such as hair, glass, smoke, and lighting.

The method offers useful controllability over foreground position and scale, supports both text-to-video and image-to-video generation, and reports substantially faster inference than TransPixeler at a higher frame count and resolution.
The VAE ablation provides consistent improvements from rendering-aware training and TABD across RGB and alpha PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS, lending some support to the component design.
weaknesses: There is a central mathematical inconsistency in the rectified-flow formulation. Equation 2 correctly defines the velocity for Z_t=t epsilon+(1-t)Z as epsilon-Z, but Equation 13 defines the modified target as Z_t-minus-epsilon, which equals (1-t)(Z-minus-epsilon) and is not the trajectory derivative. It is unclear whether this is a manuscript error or the target actually used in training; the latter would undermine the claimed rectified-flow method and the former materially harms reproducibility.

The signed TABD objective in Equation 3 multiplies a nonnegative squared error by -1 in transparent regions. Minimizing this objective directly rewards arbitrarily large prediction error and is unbounded below unless another constraint or bounded/margin formulation is used. The paper does not supply loss weights, normalization details, or a stability analysis explaining why the combined objective avoids this behavior.

The evaluation does not report the number of prompts/videos used for Table 1, the number or demographics of user-study participants, assignment and randomization procedures, handling of ties, or statistical uncertainty. This is especially consequential because transparency correctness—the central claim—is supported primarily by the user study. The transparency ranks in Table 2 also sum to 14 rather than the expected 15 for a strict five-method ranking, requiring clarification.

Most automatic metrics are computed after rendering onto a white background and therefore do not directly measure alpha accuracy, leakage, edge quality, or temporal consistency of the alpha channel. A quantitative alpha-specific evaluation on controlled or held-out compositing data would substantially strengthen the central claim.

The ablations do not quantitatively isolate the generation-level effect of TABD or the mean sampler. Table 3 only measures VAE reconstruction, while the DiT/mean-sampler evidence is qualitative. There is also no comparison against the unmodified Wan model on ordinary RGB generation to validate the claim that RGB generation ability is preserved.

Baseline fairness is difficult to assess because the methods use different base generators, sampling budgets, resolutions, and possibly training data. Thus, the large overall-quality and speed improvements cannot be attributed cleanly to the proposed distribution-learning mechanisms.

Reproducibility remains incomplete: important preprocessing, clip construction, loss reductions and weights, evaluation prompts, acceleration configuration, and training-data licensing are unspecified. The generation dataset contains only 429 selected samples, including Internet-sourced material, but its selection process and permissible redistribution are not described. Overall, the idea and reported outputs are promising, but the formulation and evaluation gaps keep the evidence near the acceptance boundary.
